To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the H1N1 influenza cases were more in pandemic period, but in post pandemic and epidemic period cases were more in older age group and with more complications.
during pandemic and recent epidemic, young age group and females were affected more and during post pandemic period older males and females having co-morbidity were more affected.
in post pandemic period, H1N1 patients were older, had more co morbid conditions, worse APACHE score on admission, more complications and higher mortality than Pandemic.
In summary, our research is concerned with
clinical and epidemiological features of H1N1 patients in pandemic, post pandemic period and recent epidemic.
the epidemiological, clinical and therapeutic profile of H1N1 patients admitted in our hospital in pandemic, post pandemic as well as recent epidemic period.
clinical epidemiology and outcomes of H1N1 influenza in a tertiary care hospital in Gujarat.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the pandemic influenza A/H1 N1 virus is a new virus which has emerged in the community and it has caused significant morbidity and mortality.
the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of H1N1 virus infection have evolved over time, and that the disease is no longer a disease of young people.
H1N1 is a serious illness with significant mortality, especially in post pandemic period, which can be prevented with early diagnosis and treatment.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the clinical and epidemiological characteristics of H1N1 influenza virus in pandemic and recent epidemic are similar but there is difference in post pandemic period which is due to the drift variants of H1N virus.
during post pandemic and recent epidemics, patients were more severe with high mortality than pandemic period.

in pandemic period young patients with no co-morbid conditions and pregnant patients are at high risk of death while in post pandemic and epidemic period older patients with co-morbid diseases and those who are delayed in seeking treatment are at high risk.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should be prepared for future epidemics of H1N1 and other influenza strains by strengthening our surveillance programmes and vaccination programmes.
the clinical and epidemiological features of H1N1 influenza are changing over time and it is important that we update our knowledge and practices accordingly.
the disease is still severe and needs to be treated early with appropriate anti viral drugs.
